title: Why quantization can break multi-step workflows
summary: Small coding experiments separate ordinary compounding, repeated repair failures and a changed token decision. They also show where the explanation stops.
body_markdown:
A model can solve almost every individual task and still complete surprisingly few workflows. In our short coding experiments, a 4-bit Qwen model passed 97.3% of tasks but only 78.1% of eight-task sequences. That difference is mostly ordinary compounding. Eight independent chances to succeed at 97.3% give roughly 80% success overall.


At 3-bit precision, the model sometimes repeated an expression after a test had already rejected it. In the clearest case, it agreed with BF16 at 14 of 15 answer positions, but one changed decision broke a boundary condition. Replacing an activation at that decision recovered correct code.


We began these experiments after[our Nemotron CQ release](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/nemotron-cq) solved seven DeepSWE tasks against the original model's 24. The experiments below use smaller models, a different quantizer and short, inspectable tasks. They demonstrate failure mechanisms that matter for multi-step work; they do not establish the cause of the Nemotron result.


## What we measured


The main model is Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. We compare BF16 with fresh MLX affine weight quantization at group size 64. Only transformer projections are quantized. Embeddings, the tied output head, norms, activations and KV-cache storage retain their original precision. All decoding is greedy unless specified otherwise.


We wrote 12 expression tasks involving indexing, rounding and bounds, then checked the answers with executable tests. There are 32 sequences of eight distinct task types, with shuffled order and renamed arguments. Each task permits three attempts, including test feedback. The conversation carries forward, but an earlier answer cannot change a later requirement. These are independent programming exercises inside a shared conversation, not edits to an evolving repository. Prompts stay within 2,102 tokens, and no generation reaches its output limit.


Repeated templates are the main statistical limitation. The tables report descriptive 95% intervals from resampling whole templates, abbreviated **T95** . With only 12 templates, these percentile intervals can be too narrow. Our primary exploratory test swaps model labels together within each template. It assumes exchangeability under the null and does not turn 12 bug families into hundreds of independent observations. **B95** denotes an exact binomial interval conditional on drawing sequences from this fixed task bank.

The rolling-history 3-bit model repeated an already-failed expression on consecutive attempts in 29 of 256 tasks, or 11.3% \[T95 3.5, 20.7\]. The corresponding counts were two for 4-bit, 0.8% \[0.0, 1.9\], and zero for BF16. Among each model's initially failed tasks, those counts are 29/82, 2/36 and 0/14. The models failed different subsets, so those conditional rates are descriptive rather than a matched comparison.

To compare repair on identical evidence, we supplied each model with the same buggy expression and the same failing tests. We wrote one mutation per template, then created eight argument-renaming variants, giving 96 entries and 67 distinct message contexts. The mutations were written after the pilot rather than copied from 3-bit outputs, although the window-boundary mutation structurally matches the pilot error. This is not an independently designed corpus of unfamiliar bugs.

Its feedback shows only one item, with batch sizes four and eight. Seven BF16 answers special-case zero items to one batch; all quantized configurations return the scorer's expected zero. ## Following one wrong token


The simplest pilot failure asks for the exclusive end of a window, capped at a total length. With start 8, size 5 and total 10, the answer must be 10. BF16 generates` min(start + size, total)` ; 3-bit generates` min(start + size, total + 1)` and returns 11.

The added term changes the contract. The 3-bit model assigns 99.92% probability to the addition token.


Figure 3.


A replay of one selected pilot example, not live inference. BF16 and 3-bit agree at 14 of 15 supplied answer positions. Most failures in the later sample have more than one disagreement.


Of 32 pilot first attempts, 3-bit failed nine. Eight had correct BF16 answers, comprising four retry cases, three alignment cases and this window case. We selected the window case during exploratory work; it was first in seed and task order, but the selection rule was not registered beforehand.


Under identical answer prefixes, the models agree on the most likely token at 14 of 15 positions. At the decisive position, BF16 puts 99.68% probability on` )` , while 3-bit puts 99.92% on` +` . This is a confident change of choice. Forcing the closing parenthesis once and then continuing normal 3-bit generation produces correct code.


Unpacking the same 3-bit weights and using dense BF16 linear operations reproduces the error. A discrepancy in the packed MLX kernel therefore cannot explain it by itself. This control concerns MLX affine quantization, not the separate CQ runtime.


We replaced one 3-bit activation with its BF16 counterpart at the input position responsible for the next-token decision. Each intervention is a separate forward pass. We swept all 36 layers for attention outputs, MLP outputs and the residual stream after the complete block. The cached prefix remains 3-bit.

Layer 22 is a clear reversal, not a near-miss concealed by a binary score. A layer-23 replacement still leaves 12 quantized blocks, layers 24–35, and they preserve the correct choice. Only replacements near the output mainly function as positive controls. At layer 35, the correct-token probability exactly equals the original BF16 value because only the unquantized final norm and head remain. This is a built-in check of the patching harness.


These results suggest a sensitive transition around layers 21–23 without identifying a single defective block. The imported state contains upstream BF16 effects, and the prefix cache remains quantized.


Layer-23 attention and layer-21 MLP replacements also recover correct completed code. Testing each at the last eight prompt positions and all 13 shared answer-prefix positions finds success only at the decision-input position. All 20 earlier positions fail for each component. A sham replacement with the original 3-bit activation leaves logits unchanged and the answer wrong.

## The clearest example is not the typical failure


We checked every fresh-history first-attempt failure with a correct matched BF16 answer. The fresh run has 85 initial 3-bit failures, distinct from the rolling run's 82. BF16's fresh first answers are correct on 64 of those 85 tasks. We compare next-token choices along those correct BF16 answers; the remaining 21 lack a correct reference and are excluded.

Only nine of 64 cases have a single disagreement, and all nine are window-boundary tasks. That is 14.1%, with nominal binomial 95% interval 6.6–25.0%; resampling the five represented templates gives a much wider 0.0–50.9%. BF16 replay matches every recorded reference token. The selected case makes an intervention easy to interpret, but most eligible failures contain several disagreements. Disagreements along a supplied reference answer are not a count of causal errors in a freely generated completion.


## Counterexamples constrain the explanation


Keeping history improves final task counts for all three Qwen configurations. BF16 rises from 253/256 to 256/256, 4-bit from 237/256 to 249/256, and 3-bit from 221/256 to 222/256. The respective paired changes are +1.2 points \[T95 0.0, 3.6\], +4.7 \[−3.1, 13.3\] and +0.4 \[−11.5, 13.1\]. Short conversation history does not explain the failures here.


A small Nemotron-4B pilot also cuts against a universal precision ranking. Over four sequences, BF16 solves 29/32 tasks and completes 2/4 sequences. The 4-bit model solves 32/32 and completes all four; 3-bit solves 23/32 and completes none. The 4-bit improvement has three paired wins and no losses, nominal p=0.25p=0.25

Even within Qwen, 4-bit fails five rolling-history backoff tasks that 3-bit passes. On repair, it solves ceiling division in 5/8 cases against 3-bit's 8/8. Precision effects depend on the task and model, not just the number of bits.

Our 3-bit and 4-bit projections therefore occupy about 3.5 and 4.5 effective bits per weight. CQ's language-backbone projections occupy 1.3814 effective bits per weight, including codes, norms, scales and shared codebooks. The complete Nemotron checkpoint is 1.418 bits per parameter. The[Cactus Quants paper](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Q6FcVpI1SO) describes the method used for that release. Equal accounting does not make different architectures, quantizers or precision allocations interchangeable.


## What this says about DeepSWE


The model card reports 24/113 BF16 successes, 21.2%, and 7/113 CQ successes, 6.2%. A saved aggregate instead records CQ as 7/110. The original paired task records were unavailable for this analysis, so we cannot resolve those three tasks or measure the overlap of successes.


Conditional on 113 common independent task pairs, the gap is 15.0 percentage points. Across all possible overlaps of the 24 and seven successes, exact McNemar pp


p


ranges from 0.0000153 to 0.00333. A conservative 95% envelope for the paired gap is 2.3–31.6 points. Even counting all three missing CQ tasks as successes gives a 12.4-point gap and a maximum paired pp


p


of 0.0243 under those assumptions.


That calculation addresses task sampling conditional on the observed runs. Each configuration appears to have only one agent run. It does not measure agent run-to-run stochasticity, and it cannot replace a second BF16 run or reconciliation of the task records. No full DeepSWE evaluation was run for this article.


The mechanisms we can demonstrate are narrower. Small per-task deficits compound across required steps. Some failed repairs repeat rather than provide independent chances. In at least one inspected case, quantized weights change a decisive computation despite high agreement elsewhere, and targeted activation replacements recover the correct answer. These effects occur in short contexts, so long context is not necessary for them. Long context may still contribute at DeepSWE lengths.


## Related work


Dong and colleagues'[ACBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19433) evaluates compressed models across workflow generation, tool use, long-context understanding and real-world applications. Its GPTQ/AWQ results distinguish relatively preserved workflow and tool-use scores from larger real-world application losses. This supports evaluating complete agent tasks separately from short-answer benchmarks; it does not identify the mechanism behind our release's DeepSWE result.


Afrin, Haque and Mastropaolo's[study of quantization for code generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14181) compares six methods on Qwen2.5-Coder and CodeLlama. It finds substantial variation by method and prompt complexity, including configurations that match or exceed the reference. PrismML's[Ternary Bonsai release limitations](https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-27B-mlx-2bit/blob/d4f586a3583b496942703df1099eac8c3fb140a9/README.md) separately caution about long-horizon coding. A release limitation is useful deployment context, not a controlled causal experiment.


Quantization methods make different choices about which errors to reduce.[GPTQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323) uses approximate second-order information for weight reconstruction;[AWQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978) uses activation-aware scaling;[QuIP#](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04396) combines Hadamard-based incoherence processing with lattice codebooks. Our controlled small-model study uses MLX affine quantization, not those methods or CQ. Its results should not be read as a ranking of quantizers.


The activation interventions follow the general logic of causal tracing, exemplified by Meng and colleagues'[work on factual associations in GPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05262) . Here the source and recipient runs differ in weight precision rather than a corrupted factual prompt. A successful replacement identifies a state sufficient to alter the chosen decision under that intervention; it does not by itself localize the responsible weight errors.


## Evidence and statistical details


The[complete plain-text analysis](https://www.cactuscompute.com/quantization/quantization_long_tasks.txt) contains the per-template results, all paired restoration comparisons, both repair cohorts, the full layer-probability table and interval construction. The[figure data](https://www.cactuscompute.com/quantization/evidence.json) provide the numerical values behind the interactive charts. Bootstrap intervals use 50,000 template resamples with seed 20261112; label-swap tests enumerate all assignments across the included templates. All comparisons remain exploratory.
